term: Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW)
match: Crime Survey for England and Wales
def: A large household survey run for the Office for National Statistics. It asks people aged 16 and over about crimes they have experienced in the past year, whether or not they reported them to the police, so it is the best guide to long-term trends in crime against households and individuals.

Offences such as scams and hacking. They are left out of the long-run comparisons here because the survey only began measuring them in 2016/17, and police figures for them are recorded nationally by Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) rather than by local forces.

Crimes reported to and recorded by the police under the Home Office Counting Rules. It reflects how readily people report and how strictly forces record, as well as how much crime happens, so its trend can differ from the Crime Survey.
Rules introduced in April 2002 to make police recording of crime more consistent and victim-focused. Recorded crime rose when they came in, so earlier figures are not comparable.
A count that adds part-time staff as fractions of a full-time post, so two officers working half-time count as one.
Uniformed police staff who patrol neighbourhoods and support officers, with more limited powers than a police officer.
The government programme announced in 2019 to recruit 20,000 additional police officers in England and Wales by March 2023.
Money values adjusted for inflation, so spending in different years can be compared at the same prices.
In most force areas, an elected commissioner who sets police priorities and the budget and holds the chief constable to account. In London and some other areas a mayor holds these powers.
The area covered by one of the 43 territorial police forces in England and Wales.
A formal decision to prosecute: the suspect is charged or summonsed to appear at court. The charge rate is the share of recorded crimes that end this way.

The main stop and search power, under section 1 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, with related powers such as those in the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971. Officers need reasonable grounds to suspect the person is carrying stolen or prohibited items, weapons or drugs.

match: times more likely if Black than if White
def: How many times higher the rate of stop and search per 1,000 people is for Black people than for White people. A ratio of 1 would mean equal rates.
The population counts used to turn numbers of searches into rates. Moving from 2011 to 2021 Census figures changed the rates even where the number of searches did not change.
Cases a court has received but not yet completed, often called the court backlog.
The court for the most serious criminal cases, heard by a judge and jury, which also deals with appeals and with cases sent from the magistrates' courts for sentence.
The courts where every criminal case starts and most are completed, heard by magistrates or a district judge without a jury.
Holding someone in prison after a court has refused bail, either before trial or after conviction while they await sentence. People remanded awaiting trial have not been convicted.

term: Useable operational capacity and spare places
def: Useable operational capacity is the number of prisoners the estate can hold without serious risk to order and safety, less a margin for cells that cannot be used on any given day. Spare places, or headroom, are that capacity minus the population.
The most common prison sentence: a fixed term, with automatic release on licence partway through and the rest served in the community under supervision, with recall to prison for breaches.

The change from September 2024 that moved automatic release for most standard determinate sentences from the halfway point to 40% of the term, to relieve prison overcrowding. Sex offences, terrorism, serious violence with sentences of four years or more and some domestic abuse offences were excluded.
An emergency scheme from October 2023 to September 2024 that released some prisoners before their automatic release date, by up to 70 days by its final months, to free prison places.

The release arrangement introduced by the Sentencing Act 2026 from 1 October 2026. Most people on standard determinate sentences are released automatically at the one-third point and some serious offences at half, with days added for breaking prison rules.

Extended determinate sentences are for offenders assessed as dangerous: release needs Parole Board approval after at least two thirds of the term, followed by an extended licence. Life sentences have no fixed release date; the Parole Board decides once the minimum term has been served.
The law that received Royal Assent on 22 January 2026. It introduced the progression model, a presumption to suspend prison sentences of 12 months or less, and wider use of community sentences.
An emergency measure that lets adult male prisoners be held temporarily in police cells when prisons are full.
An indeterminate sentence introduced in 2005 and abolished for new cases in 2012. People serving it are released only when the Parole Board agrees, however short their minimum term.
Children aged 10 to 17 receiving their first caution or conviction, and so entering the formal youth justice system.
Children under 18 held in young offender institutions, secure training centres, secure children's homes or the secure school, whether on remand or serving a sentence.
The public's belief that the police have the right to exercise authority, shown in trust, a sense that the police act fairly and lawfully, and willingness to cooperate and comply.
Concentrating patrols or other police activity on the small places, often single streets or addresses, where crime clusters.
An approach that analyses the underlying causes of a recurring crime problem, designs a response, often with partners, and then assesses whether it worked.
Displacement is crime moving to nearby places or other times when police focus on one area. Diffusion of benefits is the opposite: crime also falls in the surrounding area.
A point where the definition or method behind a statistic changed, so values before and after are not directly comparable. Shown on the charts as a dashed join.
